extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, counselors, in-house and agency PR staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations professionals on legal constraints (securities law, FTC, consumer and labor statutes, lobbying/FARA) and best/worst practices in media relations and press-release distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC restrictions on pre-registration publicity (quiet period)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC specifically prohibits the issuance of certain types of information during the period immediately prior to registration of a security, the 'quiet period' when the registration is being accomplished, and the immediate postregistration period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity that constitutes an offering or a 'prospectus' is prohibited unless in proper form and containing required information. Common compliance tactic: include disclaimers such as 'This is not an offering; offering may be made only by prospectus.' The SEC nonetheless allows routine product advertising, service brochures, quarterly/annual reports to stockholders, proxy statements, press releases about business developments, responses to public inquiries, and other generally accepted publicity practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form 10-K annual report requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An annual report must be prepared using SEC Form 10-K no later than ninety days after the close of the company's fiscal year (and the SEC has complex rules for interim quarterly reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations often packages required disclosures into a glossy annual report resembling a magazine, but must include all required SEC information. Be aware the SEC may expand 10-K requirements to require discussion of unfavorable trends, explanation of sales predictions, and detailed departmental or divisional information (continuous disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely disclosure (no selective timing/routing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure must be timely, which means a release must be disseminated as soon as information is known, not when the company feels it will have the most desirable effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manipulate timing or routing of releases to favor some potential investors over others. NYSE guidance: releases should be phoned or delivered immediately to major wire services and Dow Jones; 'hold for release' announcements should not be used. Timely disclosure prevents insiders (including PR staff) from profiting on undisclosed material information (Texas Gulf Sulphur case cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid compensation-in-stock conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unethical for the PR practitioner to be compensated for services in connection with a new stock offering in shares instead of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRSA's code of professional standards holds that accepting stock compensation creates a conflict of duty to client, employer, or the investing public; avoid equity-based compensation tied to offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC deceptive advertising standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC (Section 5 of the FTC Act) broadly outlaws 'unfair or deceptive acts in commerce'; 'deceptive advertising' can be any statement, claim, or pictorial demonstration that may have the capacity or tendency to deceive the average man on the street.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency need only prove capacity to deceive, not actual deception. Deceptive claims include misrepresentation of product efficacy, size/shape/weight/origin, unauthorized or untrue testimonials, false disparagement of competitors, ambiguous statements. PR should avoid such claims in ads and news releases; consult FTC guidelines and advisory opinions when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC scrutiny of news releases for false product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC is particularly alert to false claims about products or services, and it looks at news releases as well as advertisements for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-risk claims include assertions that a product is original/first, approved by a government agency, patented, developed in a nonexistent research laboratory, has nonexistent nutritional content, or proven effectiveness beyond bona fide limits. If investigated, companies may be offered consent decrees — PR counsel should advise on whether to agree or litigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consent decrees with FTC as PR decision point
rubrics_metrics.description: A consent order agreement permits the company to change its advertising or promotional practices in line with the FTC’s suggestions in order to end the matter and resume favorable promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing a consent decree can shorten exposure but may produce adverse publicity; involve PR counsel to manage communications and reputation during and after settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) disclosure and consumer-rights requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCPA requires disclosures in consumer credit transactions, provides mechanisms for resolving billing errors, restricts certain debt-collection activities, and prohibits credit discrimination on bases such as sex, marital status, race, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lending institutions should designate a consumer compliance officer and establish a compliance task force and procedures to handle consumer complaints and disseminate notices about company policies that comply with the Consumer Act. Public relations personnel are usually instrumental in designing and communicating these procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish consumer-compliance procedures and designate officer
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental step for lending institutions is to designate one person as a 'consumer compliance officer' to train personnel and oversee a compliance task force; procedures must be established to handle consumer complaints and disseminate compliance notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR typically helps draft procedures and public-facing notices; ensure internal training and external communications align with legal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee labor-rights compliance (NLRB/Wagner Act/Taft-Hartley/landrum-griffin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must not interfere with the workings of labor unions or the rights of employees to bargain; certain employer communications (threats of reprisals or promises of benefits) are unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR-written speeches delivered to employees that contain threats or promises are unlawful; noncoercive talks by employees to fellow employees on company time/property are permitted. PR must coordinate with labor counsel to avoid unfair labor-practice exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employees' right to clear and complete information
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees have a basic right to clear and complete information; failure to provide full explanation of retirement or insurance benefits, for example, may result in judgments against the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR should ensure internal communications about benefits and policies are full, accurate, and documented; consider ombudsmen or privacy/bill-of-rights style documents to manage employee concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and manage OSHA and safety-related publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA orders create public-relations headaches; PR must attempt to avoid adverse publicity by anticipating violations and working to ensure the company avoids being fined or put on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When violations occur, PR should push management to correct problems promptly and develop corrective, transparent communications to minimize negative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: EEOC and sexual-harassment policy expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: EEOC guidelines suggest firms with government contracts should draw up company policies on sexual harassment, creating work for the PR department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR should help develop and communicate anti-harassment policies and training to comply with EEOC expectations and prevent reputational risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower protections and employee-grievance mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1978, rights of federal employees who 'blow the whistle' have been protected; some companies publish a 'bill of rights' for employee privacy and use ombudsmen to hear grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR should support whistleblower channels and internal grievance mechanisms to maintain trust and reduce public fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying registration and reporting (Federal Regulation of Lobbying Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Regulation of Lobbying Act of 1946 requires those representing interests in Washington to register and file quarterly reports of significant sources of income and expenditures; it also aims to include organizations that initiate letter/telegram campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusions: news media, elected officials, persons testifying before committees. Over half of states have their own lobbying controls; organizations should contact each state's secretary of state to determine registration needs before initiating campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents representing foreign organizations or governments must disclose activities and finances, properly identify themselves when dealing with legislators or government officials, and open their books to government inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration under FARA does not limit activities but requires transparency; compliance avoids legal exposure and public scandal. Enforcement historically uneven, but disclosure is mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative relationship with legal counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations and law must approach their relationship constructively; PR and lawyers share common goals to serve the client and public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners should depend on counsel to guide them through complex regulations and precedents; coordinate early with legal when legal trouble is anticipated to plan an 'aggressive campaign, forehanded, educational and flexible' to adjust to court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat media as gatekeepers and manage interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The media serve as 'gatekeepers,' controlling the information that flows to other publics; media workers process information and pass it on, so their behavior sets limits on what publics receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media relations is central but not the whole of PR. Recognize the interdependence: PR supplies reporters with information they cannot feasibly gather on their own; manage relationships to serve the broader public-information system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align PR output with journalists' primary news values (accuracy & reader interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists rank 'accuracy' and 'interest to the reader' as the two top news values; PR practitioners should prioritize these to be effective sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid practices journalists see as self-serving (pseudo-events, 'publicity disguised as news'); ensure releases are accurate, relevant to readers, and not merely designed to depict the subject favorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promises to 'deliver' the media
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises to 'deliver' the media (i.e., guaranteeing placements) are decried by journalists and damage PR credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not guarantee or promise media placement as a selling point to clients or management; such promises provoke editors and erode relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not condition coverage by threatening or buying advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats to withhold advertising if editors do not use an item, or a promise to buy advertising if they do use it, are abusive tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leveraging advertising dollars to influence editorial choices; this blurs ethical lines and may result in refused access or reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid calling executives to pressure reporters or editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling an executive of a newspaper or broadcast station to pressure a reporter or editor to use a story is an abusive practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use high-level pressure to influence editorial decisions; cultivate professional contacts and build trust rather than exert coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't send reams of news releases with little news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending reams of news releases with little news value to an extensive mailing list of media that have no use for them is a press-agentry abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target distribution to outlets for whom the content is relevant; avoid mass blasts designed to 'look busy' to superiors or clients. Tailor releases and respect editors' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'more releases = more pickups' mass-saturation belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the attitude that the more releases sent, the greater the chance they will be used (belief that editors pick randomly when they have space) is misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on quality, relevance, and timing rather than volume. Excessive quantity creates clutter and alienates journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't cater to television at the expense of print media
rubrics_metrics.description: Catering to television at the expense of the print media (especially at press conferences) is a harmful practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the needs of different media platforms; prepare materials and events that serve multiple outlets or provide tailored content rather than privileging one medium to the detriment of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mailing releases to out-of-town media with no local relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mailing releases to out-of-town media when the information has no local relevance to those media is ineffective and annoying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate geographically relevant outreach; identify which outlets have jurisdictional or topical interest before distributing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not send multiple copies of the same release to different departments at the same outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending multiple copies of the same release to different departments or individuals in the same publication or broadcast outlet is wasteful and counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the correct desk or contact and send one tailored copy; multiple copies clutter newsrooms and reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disclaimers and routine publicity to maintain visibility during SEC-regulated periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC recognizes the need to maintain normal visibility during registration periods and does not prohibit certain routine publicity; firms often use disclaimers (e.g., 'This is not an offering; offering may be made only by prospectus') as compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing allowed publicity (product ads, brochures, reports, proxy statements, certain press releases), craft messaging to avoid constituting an improper prospectus; consult legal to ensure compliance with form/content requirements.
